title: Eid al-Adha: days of tashriq
hook: takbir after prayers for the days after Eid

segments.voice: Yesterday, Dhul Hijjah, and your line was the best ten days. Did you mark your first small good somewhere, so the next day could find it? Day five hundred fourteen.

In a lot of Muslim homes, the morning of Eid al-Adha has a particular sound. Not just greetings and children, but bags. Plastic bags of meat being divided on the kitchen counter, knotted, labeled, carried next door, driven across town, dropped at a cousin's, handed to the man who sweeps the street. Phones buzzing with addresses. Someone always asking whether the neighbors on the third floor got theirs. It's the feast of the sacrifice, and it doesn't end in one day. Today: Eid al-Adha, and the days that follow it.
screen: `A FEAST THAT DOESN'T END IN A DAY.`

segments.voice: Eid al-Adha falls on the tenth of Dhul Hijjah, the day after the pilgrims stand at 'Arafah. It remembers Ibrahim, who in Surah As-Saffat saw in a dream that he was to sacrifice his son, and both of them submitted, and God ransomed the son with a tremendous sacrifice. Muslims who are able offer an animal, a sheep, a goat, a share in a cow or camel, and the Qur'an tells them in Surah Al-Hajj to eat of it and to feed the one who is content and the one who asks. Many divide it in thirds: for the household, for friends and neighbors, and for those in need, a custom scholars recommend rather than require. The same surah adds a line often quoted at Eid: neither the flesh nor the blood reaches God; what reaches Him is your devotion, your taqwa. Then come three more days, the eleventh, twelfth and thirteenth, called the days of tashriq. A hadith in Sahih Muslim describes them in a phrase that became today's line: they are days of eating and drinking, and of remembering God. Fasting is not allowed on them. And the remembrance has a shape. Surah Al-Baqarah says to remember God through the numbered days, and many Muslims say the takbir after each of the five daily prayers, from the dawn of 'Arafah until the afternoon of the thirteenth. It begins: God is greatest, God is greatest, there is no god but God. The schools differ a little on the exact start and end. So a feast, a share for the neighbor, and a refrain after every prayer, across the four days of the feast.
screen: `THE TENTH: IBRAHIM'S RANSOM.` · `EAT, AND FEED THE ONE WHO ASKS.` · `NOT THE FLESH: THE DEVOTION.` · `THREE DAYS OF TASHRIQ.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: share food with a neighbor. Sit, and let the breath settle. Picture the people who live closest to you. The door across the hall, the house over the fence, the colleague at the next desk. Pick one, maybe someone you've never really spoken to. Decide what you could bring them this week. It needn't be meat or anything grand. A plate of something you cooked, a box of fruit, tea you like. Picture handing it over. If you pray, you can say God is greatest, quietly, as you imagine it. The bell holds the time.
Eid al-Adha. The feast of the sacrifice on the tenth of Dhul Hijjah, remembering Ibrahim's ransom, followed by the three days of tashriq. Today's word.
Your line: eat, drink, remember. Today, at one meal, before you eat, stop for one breath and remember where it came from. Day five hundred fourteen.

howItsDone: On Eid al-Adha Muslims who are able offer an animal sacrifice and share the meat with family, neighbors and people in need; many say the takbir after the daily prayers through the days of tashriq, the eleventh to thirteenth of Dhul Hijjah.

myth: the days of tashriq are good days for a voluntary fast
the hadith calls them days of eating, drinking and remembering God; fasting isn't allowed.
the Qur'an says the sacrifice's flesh and blood don't reach God
Surah Al-Hajj says what reaches Him is the devotion.
dividing the meat in thirds is a strict obligation
it's a common custom that scholars recommend, not a requirement.

original.note: Arabic: the days of tashriq, the three days after Eid al-Adha, the eleventh to the thirteenth of Dhul Hijjah.

trapdoor: what you thought: the festival where Muslims sacrifice a sheep.
what it means: a feast remembering Ibrahim's ransom, where the meat is shared outward, and three more days of eating, drinking and remembrance.
what a scholar hears: As-Saffat 37:102–107; Al-Hajj 22:28, 36–37; Al-Baqarah 2:203's numbered days; and Muslim 1141 on the days of tashriq.

sources.ref: Qur'an 22:36–37 (eat and feed; the devotion reaches Him)
Qur'an 2:203 (remember God through the numbered days)
Sahih Muslim 1141 (days of eating, drinking and remembrance)

notes: No direct quotations; Qur'an and hadith paraphrased. Muslim 1141 (Nubayshah al-Hudhali) cited from memory; confirm.
The derivation of adha (from the forenoon sacrifice) and of tashriq (drying meat in the sun) are the common explanations; others exist. Confirm.
The takbir after prayers 'from the dawn of 'Arafah until the afternoon of the thirteenth' is a widely held view; schools differ on start and end, as the script says. Confirm the takbir wording given.
The son's name is not given in 37:102; the script leaves him unnamed. Most Muslims understand him as Isma'il.
Thirds division described as a recommendation; confirm.

Editor review (2026-10-01): removed the unsourced derivations of adha and tashriq (teach and original); 'people quote every year' softened; the takbir is now introduced as 'it begins', since the common formula continues past the words given; 'four days running' clarified (the takbir itself starts on 'Arafah). Keeper: Bukhari allows some pilgrims without a sacrificial animal to fast on the days of tashriq; the script's 'fasting is not allowed' is the general rule.
